name: Inversion: Never have I…, Not only did she…
subtitle: After a negative or limiting adverbial at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject: Never have I seen such a mess. Not only did she win, she broke the record. It is formal and written, or used for strong emphasis.
source: icanspeak Spanish original English text (grammar-c1 run, 2026-10-29)

concept.exampleHtml: Never have I seen such a mess. — Not only did she win, she broke the record. — Had I known, I would have called.

qa.html: Word order: when a negative or limiting adverbial opens the sentence, the word order is like a question: auxiliary + subject + main verb. I have never seen such a mess. → Never have I seen such a mess. She rarely complains. → Rarely does she complain.

Which auxiliary? Use the auxiliary of the tense: Never have I seen… (present perfect), Never had I seen… (past perfect), Never will I forget… (future), Under no circumstances must you… (modal). If the verb has no auxiliary, add do, does or did: Rarely does she complain. Little did he know. The verb be moves itself: Never was he so happy.

Which adverbials? Never, rarely, seldom, little, nowhere · hardly / barely / scarcely … when · no sooner … than · not only … but also · not until · only when / only after / only then · under no circumstances, on no account, at no time, in no way. With two clauses, only the first one is inverted: Hardly had she sat down when the phone rang. — No sooner had he left than it began to rain.

Without if: in formal writing you can drop if and put the auxiliary first. If I had known… → Had I known, I would have called. — If you should need help… → Should you need help, call me. — If it were not for the rain… → Were it not for the rain, we would go. The negative stays in full: Had I not been so tired…
So … that / Such was…: So loud was the music that nobody could talk. — Such was his anger that he walked out. This is a literary, formal pattern. The ordinary form is The music was so loud that…

Typical mistakes: ✗ Never I have seen such a mess. → ✓ Never have I seen such a mess. · ✗ Rarely she complains. → ✓ Rarely does she complain. · ✗ No sooner had he left when it rained. → ✓ No sooner had he left than it rained. (no sooner … than, hardly … when)

concept.noteHtml: Inversion belongs to formal, written English: reports, speeches, literature. In speech you hear it mostly for strong emphasis. The adverbial must be at the front: I have never seen it has normal order. In Only when she called did I understand and Not until midnight did they arrive, the inversion is in the main clause, not in the when or until part. Not only … but also is explained in Paired conjunctions. Had I known is the third conditional: see Third and mixed conditionals; wish. The simpler conditionals are in Conditionals 0, 1, 2.

tables.caption: Normal order and inverted order
head: Normal order
With inversion
rows: I have never seen such a mess.
Never {have I} seen such a mess.
She rarely complains.
Rarely {does she} complain.
We had hardly sat down when the film started.
Hardly {had we} sat down when the film started.
He didn't know what was coming.
Little {did he} know what was coming.
She not only won, she broke the record.
Not only {did she} win, she broke the record.
He realised the truth only later.
Only later {did he} realise the truth.
You must not open this door under any circumstances.
Under no circumstances {must you} open this door.

tables.caption: Patterns and examples
head: Adverbial
Pattern
Example
rows: Never, rarely, seldom
+ auxiliary + subject + verb
Seldom {do we} see such talent.
Hardly / barely / scarcely … when
had + subject + past participle … when
Hardly {had I} arrived when it began to rain.
No sooner … than
had + subject + past participle … than
No sooner {had she} left than he called.
Not only … but also
Not only + auxiliary + subject
Not only {is the hotel} cheap, but it is also clean.
Not until / only when
inversion in the main clause
Not until midnight {did they} arrive.
Under no circumstances, on no account, at no time
+ auxiliary / modal + subject
Under no circumstances {should you} open it.
Little
did + subject + verb
Little {did she} know.

tables.caption: Conditional inversion: with and without if
head: With if
Without if (formal)
rows: If I had known, I would have called.
{Had I} known, I would have called.
If you should need help, call me.
{Should you} need help, call me.
If it were not for the rain, we would go.
{Were it} not for the rain, we would go.
If I hadn't been so tired, I would have stayed.
{Had I not} been so tired, I would have stayed.

be moves: Never was he so happy.
Modals move too: Under no circumstances must you…

Everyday: I've never seen such a mess.

listen.text: Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset.
listen.note: Never + have + I: the auxiliary comes before the subject.

listen.text: Not only did she pass, she got the top mark.
listen.note: Not only + did + she + base form.

listen.text: Had I known about the delay, I would have left earlier.
listen.note: Had I known = If I had known (formal).

hoeren.instruction: Listen and choose the words you hear. Listen for the order of the auxiliary and the subject.

items.text: Hardly had we arrived when it started to rain.
Under no circumstances should you open the door.
choices: Under no circumstances you should open
Under no circumstances should you open
Under no circumstances should open you

items.text: Not until midnight did the guests leave.
choices: Not until midnight the guests left
Not until midnight did the guests leave
Not until midnight left the guests

items.text: Were it not for your help, I would still be stuck.
Little did she know what was waiting for her.

rounds.label: 1 · Start with the adverb
rounds.instruction: You hear a normal sentence and an adverb in brackets. Say the sentence again, starting with the adverb and changing the word order.

example.prompt: I have never seen such a crowd. (never)
example.answer: Never have I seen such a crowd.

items.answer: Rarely does she ask for help.

items.prompt: We had hardly sat down when the lights went out. (hardly)
items.answer: Hardly had we sat down when the lights went out.
Little did she realise the danger.

items.prompt: I have seldom felt so tired. (seldom)
items.answer: Seldom have I felt so tired.

items.prompt: You must not touch this button under any circumstances. (under no circumstances)
items.answer: Under no circumstances must you touch this button.

items.prompt: I have never been so embarrassed. (never)
items.answer: Never have I been so embarrassed.

rounds.label: 2 · Drop the if
rounds.instruction: You hear a sentence with if. Say it again without if, in a formal way.

example.prompt: If I had known, I would have called.
example.answer: Had I known, I would have called.

items.prompt: If you should need help, please ask.
items.answer: Should you need help, please ask.

items.prompt: If she had left earlier, she would have caught the train.
items.answer: Had she left earlier, she would have caught the train.

items.prompt: If it were not for the noise, I would stay.
items.answer: Were it not for the noise, I would stay.

items.prompt: If they had told us, we would have helped.
items.answer: Had they told us, we would have helped.

items.prompt: If you should have any questions, call me.
items.answer: Should you have any questions, call me.

items.prompt: If I were in your position, I would apply.
items.answer: Were I in your position, I would apply.

exercises.title: Which auxiliary?
exercises.hint: Look at the tense of the rest of the sentence: the auxiliary must match it.

exercises.title: Complete with inversion.
exercises.hint: After the adverb, put the auxiliary before the subject.

exercises.title: What goes together?
exercises.hint: Tap the inverted sentence, then the normal sentence with the same meaning.

exercises.title: when or than?
exercises.hint: hardly / barely / scarcely go with when. No sooner goes with than.

exercises.title: Gap text: A letter of complaint
exercises.hint: Formal inversion. Which word comes before the subject, or links the two parts?
